## IAM-Atlas v2.1: a reference built and checked as a calibrated map

IAM-Atlas v2.1 joins two bodies of method that developed apart. Genomics built the assays, the reference cell types and the deconvolution that read a cell's methylation; cosmology built the statistics that turn many noisy, differently calibrated scans of one faint signal into a single map with a stated uncertainty at every point. Each field built its toolkit because its data demanded it, and neither had reason to borrow the other's.

The atlas applies the second toolkit to the first field's data, because both problems are the same kind of problem: a faint signal at hundreds of thousands of positions, read through instruments that each carry their own offset, where the value at each position is only as useful as its stated uncertainty.

This is not a bigger table built for the sake of putting more cells in one place. A blended 79-cell atlas with MCMC posteriors would be interesting, but not new. What is new is how it was built and how it was checked: the way cosmologists build and check a map of the sky. That is what we mean by the information physics of the methylome, and every tool below is something a geneticist can use in their own work, not only in ours.

### The tools, in IAM-Atlas v2.1

| tool | in cosmology | in IAM-Atlas v2.1 | IAM-Atlas's unique capability |
|---|---|---|---|
| **One map from many instruments** | Planck's sky maps were made by fitting every scan from every detector together, with each scan's own offset fitted alongside the sky (destriping). | 21 sources, arrays and sequencing from many laboratories, are fitted together in one hierarchical model. Each laboratory's offset is fitted apart from the cells, so the same cell measured by two laboratories becomes one cell, not two. | One reference across laboratories and platforms, instead of one table per laboratory. |
| **The whole posterior, sampled (MCMC)** | Cosmologists estimate the parameters of the universe from the microwave background by Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling, which returns every answer with its full uncertainty. | The No-U-Turn sampler fitted 813,951 array sites in 700 blocks. Every site and cell carries its best value, its 95 % range, the number of observations behind it, and the posterior draws themselves (100 per block): 60,687,175 measured cell-site values. | An error bar on every reference value, and draws that carry the reference's own uncertainty into any deconvolution or marker search built on it. |
| **A convergence certificate at every site** | No cosmological chain is reported without its Gelman-Rubin statistic (R-hat), the check that the sampler has settled. | R-hat and the effective sample size are stored for every site and cell. 0.42 % of values sit at R-hat 1.01 or above, and the whole fit had 13 divergent transitions in 700 blocks. Flagged values are kept, with the flag. | You know which reference values to trust before you use them. |
| **Masks, never filling** | Where the galaxy hides the sky, cosmologists mask it rather than paint it over. | Where a cell's sources never measured a site, the value is left blank (not measured), never imputed, and the count of observations sits beside every value. | No invented reference value slips into a deconvolution. |
| **Sample variance: the next person, not only the average** | Cosmic variance is the spread a different sky would show: how well the average is known is a different question from how much one realization varies. | The fit separates how well each cell's average is known from how much a new person's cell varies around it (the donor spread), at every site. | A range for a new person's cells, not just an error on the mean. Our deconvolution tool already reads it. |
| **Cross-calibrating two instruments** | Planck's maps were compared with WMAP's on the same sky, and a calibration difference between the two telescopes was traced and resolved. | Arrays and sequencing measure the same mark in two different ways, and the two do not agree along a straight line. On 767,672 sites measured both ways in the same 17 cell types, the relation turned out to be S-shaped, differing by up to 0.08 at the low end. IAM-Atlas v2.1 translates between the two with one measured curve that always stays between 0 and 1, tested on planted data before the fit. | Array and sequencing data read against one reference, on one scale. A conversion along a straight line carries an error of up to 0.08; IAM-Atlas v2.1 carries the measured curve itself. |
| **Blind analysis and sealed bars** | Modern microwave-background and dark-energy analyses are blinded: the tests are fixed before anyone sees the answer. | Every commissioning bar was sealed before the atlas existed, on held-out laboratories that share no GEO contributor with any source, and each use was scored once. | A reference whose claims were fixed before the data could flatter it. |
| **Tested on held-out skies** | A map earns trust on data that played no part in making it. | Held-out cells from independent laboratories, the blind sites of the tissue tests, and head-to-heads against the two published reference atlases of human cell types, one built on arrays and one on sequencing, on the jobs each was built for: three of three bars met against each. | Evidence on independent samples, not on the training data. |

What the sphere gives over a flat map: every pixel the same area, so no part of the genome is stretched; no edges or seams; genome neighbors share small patches, so clustered change shows as patches and scattered noise as speckle; and the sky's masks apply unchanged. A spectrum on this map measures order along the genome's address, which is bookkeeping, not the order a cell holds: spectra belong to the information sphere. | **The Array Information Sphere** | Cosmologists place what they measure on a sphere where distance means something physical, then read its structure with spherical statistics. | The atlas's sites placed by how their methylation varies across the cell types, not by genome address: sites that behave alike sit close together. Its rule keeps the sites measured in all 79 cell types that differ between them: 191,458 of the atlas's sites. The sky's spectra and clustering statistics belong on this sphere. |
| **The guidebook** | Every tool above, with its origin and history in cosmology. | How each tool applies to the methylome, how it differs from what geneticists use now (such as the bootstrap), and its limits. ### The tools, on the horizon

| tool | in cosmology | in IAM-Atlas v2.1 | IAM-Atlas's unique capability |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Two half-atlases and null maps** | Planck's half-mission split: two maps from two halves of the data; their difference must be pure noise. | The atlas refitted on two sealed halves of every cell's donors; half A minus half B is a noise map with no signal in it. | A direct test of the atlas's stated noise, and noise-free cross-spectra. Built on the IAM Sequencing Atlas, where the donors' sealed halves and a read-half split give two noise maps (its own chapter of the book): the read-half map fits its shuffled null (at most one band above it) in 56 of 56 cells, as pure counting noise should, and the donor-half map stands above its null in more than one band in 48 of the 48 cells with donors to split, which measures how much healthy people of one cell type differ; on IAM-Atlas v2.1 the two half fits are still to run. |
| **Power spectra, simulations and higher-order statistics** | Masked power spectra with shuffled nulls, end-to-end simulations that measure the pipeline's own transfer function, and three-point and Minkowski statistics of the residuals. | The same statistics on the atlas maps, each against its simulated null, and the cross-site covariance of healthy donors. | Structure in healthy methylation that a table of means cannot show. Built on the IAM Sequencing Atlas: the genome-distance spectrum, the healthy covariance, the transfer function, isotropy and the Minkowski functionals (its own chapter of the book). |

### What makes IAM's atlases a ruler for healthy, and could any published atlas be used instead?

Most published methylation atlases are built for deconvolution: they answer which cells are in a sample, and for that they need the average level of each cell type at a set of marker sites. IAM's instruments ask a different question: has this sample's held pattern drifted from healthy, by more than a healthy sample of the same cell mix, measured the same way, would drift? A table of averages cannot answer that, because the drift IAM measures lives in what the averages throw away. A ruler for healthy has to keep it.

- **Every site, never filled in.** IAM-Atlas v2.1 holds 813,951 array sites and the IAM Sequencing Atlas all 28,217,448 CpGs of the genome, not a selected marker set. Where a cell was never measured the site is left blank, never imputed.
- **How healthy people vary, not only their average.** Each site carries the spread between healthy donors (v2.1's donor spread; the sequencing atlas's per-donor disorder), so the edges of Normal are measured, not assumed.
- **The raw counts, so the expectation fits each sample.** A shallow sample shows more disorder from counting alone. Because the sequencing atlas keeps every donor's read counts, the chain computes what a healthy sample would show at that sample's own depth and in its own cell mix. Averages cannot do this.
- **Each source's offset measured, not blended in.** IAM-Atlas v2.1 was fitted across 21 sources with each source's offset estimated alongside the cell values, the way a sky map is built from many detectors, with every value's uncertainty and a convergence check at every site.
- **Fixed, published and checked on every run.** Both atlases are on Zenodo with checksums. Every run of the chain checks them before reading anything and stops if a file differs, and every result records the atlas it was read against.

Any atlas whose per-donor raw data are public can be rebuilt into a ruler the same way, by the chain's own build command. The IAM Sequencing Atlas is exactly that: it is rebuilt from the per-donor files of the published sequencing atlas of normal human cell types, whose work it rests on and credits. An atlas published only as a table of averages can serve the Deconvolver, but it cannot say whether a sample is healthy.

MCMC is not what makes an atlas a ruler: the IAM Sequencing Atlas is counted, not sampled. What makes either one a ruler is keeping the counts, the spread between people and the measurement terms, then fixing the result so everyone reads against the same one.

Who the donors were, for every group both atlases are built from, from each source's own record and paper (tables `seq_atlas_donor_sources.csv`, `atlas_v21_donor_sources.csv` and `atlas_v2_groups_donor_sources.csv` in Biological_Physics/MethylPhys/doors/data/DEV_ATLAS_V21_01/, the first under seq_atlas/):

- **IAM Sequencing Atlas:** 156 donor files, 57 cells: 119 are normal tissue left over from clinically needed surgery for something else, taken away from any known disease and confirmed with the surgeons or pathologists; 20 come from deceased organ donors and islet programs; 9 from adipose surgery and brain autopsies; 8 are commercial primary cells. Ages 3 to 83, median 52. Every cell type was purified by sorting and its purity checked. The 58th column, megakaryocytes, is provisional: built from single megakaryocytes of two healthy donors (33 and 19 cells), sequenced one cell at a time, because no healthy bulk megakaryocyte sequencing is open.
- **IAM-Atlas v2.1, groups carried from v2:** two sorted-blood reference libraries from healthy volunteers (37 donors screened for no history of heart, lung or kidney disease, asthma, blood disorders, autoimmune disease, cancer or diabetes; 56 anonymous healthy donors); an array cell reference made mostly of normal tissue from surgery; three adult post-mortem brains, their health not described in the text read.
- **IAM-Atlas v2.1, its 15 new sources (472 arrays):** 150 arrays from healthy volunteers or donors; 133 from the healthy control groups of disease studies (only the controls were used); 60 from a population twin cohort, all aged 19, not selected for disease; 88 from blood donors whose health is not otherwise described; 16 normal ovarian and tubal tissue from surgical patients without cancer; 16 children's normal intestinal tissue; 9 embryonic stem cell lines.

No source is a study's comparison group taken on its label, and none is tissue beside a tumor. The accurate description is healthy or verified-normal donors, purified to single cell types, not a cohort of people free of disease: most sequencing-atlas donors were having surgery for something else. Where a source says less about its donors, the tables say so.

**Why is the atlas the only healthy reference, and not healthy samples run beside the sample?**

Two questions are kept apart. What does healthy look like? That comes only from the atlases, built from cells of healthy donors so that healthy is certain; never from other samples in the same run, laboratory or study, which are only labeled healthy and can carry the very signal being looked for. What did the instrument do to this measurement? That is calibration, a different job, answered by calibrators whose answer is already known, never by the sample's neighbors. Clinical laboratories calibrate this way: reference DNA of known methylation (fully methylated, unmethylated and mixes of the two) is run beside each sample, and it tells what the instrument did without saying what healthy is. Cosmology keeps the same separation: the sky model comes from the theory, and each detector is calibrated on sources whose answer is already known, never on the signal being measured. For public data, the atlas's donors play the calibrators' part: the same healthy cell types, measured in many laboratories, show what laboratories do to a measurement, and each cell's Normal width is measured from them. And because nothing is borrowed from the sample's neighbors, nothing the instrument does can cancel unseen: every reading compares like with like, against a reference that is certainly healthy.

**Why must the atlas go through the same processing as the sample?**

Because a comparison is fair only when both sides have passed through the same instrument and the same pipeline. Cosmologists work this way: they do not clean the instrument out of the data before comparing it with theory; they pass the theory, as simulated skies, through a model of the same instrument and the same processing (beams, filtering, masks, map-making), compare the data with theory processed identically, and carry the reference's own uncertainty (noise maps, half-mission maps, null tests) into every comparison. The atlas is used the same way. It is built from public data of purified healthy cells, and it serves as the model of healthy with its own measured uncertainty, compared to a sample only after both have taken the same path. On arrays, the atlas's donor arrays were calibrated from their raw files by the chain's own first stage, the stage every sample goes through, and each array's own measured response is then applied to the atlas before the comparison (the healthy prediction). On sequencing, the calls at the two ends of a DNA molecule carry the laboratory's library chemistry, a bias long known in bisulfite sequencing; so the IAM Sequencing Atlas is being counted again from its donors' molecules exactly as a sample is read, and tested on libraries from several laboratories.

**What is commissioned.** IAM-Atlas v2.1 is commissioned use by use, each on its own sealed test: as the reference for cortical neurons, lung bronchus epithelium and naive CD4 T cells; as the source of the blind sites in the colon and lung tissue tests; and, read by the IAM-Deconvolver, for the blood-cell shares of neutrophils, monocytes, CD4 and CD8 T cells (mean share error 0.016 on mixtures from a laboratory the atlas never saw). Every one of its 813,951 sites is keyed both to its array probe and to its CpG position in the published sequencing atlas, so array and sequencing tools open the same atlas. Its values are on the array scale (its sequencing sources are placed on that scale), and it is the ruler for arrays; sequenced samples read against the IAM Sequencing Atlas, counted from sequencing reads, because an array never quite reads 0 or 1 and sequencing does.

**The IAM Sequencing Atlas (in development).** Each kind of instrument reads the same biology through its own chemistry. An array reads a probe's light, which never quite reaches 0 or 1: a site no cell ever marks still reads at the array's floor, a few percent up. Sequencing counts reads, so the same site reads about 0. Healthy disorder is computed from those levels, and near the floor a small offset in level is a large offset in disorder; the offset also changes with each laboratory's chemistry and library. So each kind of instrument reads against a ruler measured with its own chemistry: arrays against IAM-Atlas v2.1, sequenced samples against the IAM Sequencing Atlas. The physics and the instruments are the same; only the ruler changes with the platform. Read against IAM-Atlas v2.1, healthy sequenced samples showed it: at the islands every healthy cell keeps unmarked they read about 14 where healthy reads 1, and Met-A followed each sample's source. IAM-Atlas v2.1 is the ruler for arrays. Sequenced samples now have a ruler of their own, kept apart from it, so nothing built for sequencing can move an array reading. The IAM Sequencing Atlas holds, for each of 58 healthy cell types (megakaryocytes provisional) and at every one of the 28.2 million CpGs of the genome numbering sequencing uses, the healthy level, the spread between donors, each donor's own measured disorder, the reads behind each value, and two noise maps carried over from the sky: one from splitting the donors into sealed halves, one from splitting every donor's reads in two, which stands in where a cell has a single donor. Each cell has reads at 97 to 98 % of all CpGs, about thirty-two times the sites an array reads. Nothing in it is fitted: every value is counted from healthy donors' reads, and the whole atlas rebuilds from the public files with one command in minutes. What it gives the instruments is the healthy disorder of the sample's own cell type at every CpG, so a sequenced sample's departures can be read across the whole genome, including clusters far from any array site. Read against it, every healthy sequenced input reads Normal on every reading, 140 of 140: sorted-cell Met-A 1.0075, the islands 1.0118, the domains 1.0014. In development: each cell is commissioned when healthy sequenced samples it has never held read Normal against it. Each library's own floor is measured too: the physical floor is set by the energy that holds a mark, a laboratory's chemistry adds its own small rate of false ``methylated'' calls on top of it, and the chain measures that rate in every sequenced sample at the sites no healthy cell marks and reads it as a property of the library, not of the cell. The IAM Sequencing Atlas has its own chapter (its own chapter of the book) and its own Zenodo record (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24051846).

*Methods built to map a faint signal on a sphere, applied to the cell, because the same statistics serve both records.*

# IAM-Atlas v2.1: compact copy

The fitted atlas (2026-10-16): 79 cell types, 813,951 array sites, from the Bayesian fit of record `../../doors/DEV_ATLAS_V21_01.md`.
**Commissioned use by use** (`../../doors/COMMISSIONING_NOTE_ATLAS_V21.md`): three cell reference profiles and the blind sites of the colon and lung tissue tests; every other use is labeled development until it passes its own sealed test.

| File | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `sites.parquet` | every site id, in the row order of the tables below |
| `mu_part1-3.parquet` | best estimate (posterior mean) per site and cell; columns are the cells, in the source atlases' exact names |
| `mu_lo_part1-3.parquet`, `mu_hi_part1-3.parquet` | the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles (the 95 % range of the cell's average) |
| `donor_sd_part1-3.parquet` | the fit's person-to-person spread of each cell at each site (posterior mean of the donor SD); a new person's cell varies this much around the average |
| `sites_sequencing_key.parquet` | the same sites in sequencing coordinates: Illumina probe ID, the CpG index of the published sequencing atlas's .beta files (Loyfer et al. 2023, GSE186458; wgbstools numbering, 1-based; all 813,951 sites keyed, none shared), and the manifest chromosome and position (hg19). Join it to any table above to open the atlas in sequencing tools at these sites |
| `compact_manifest.json` | each file's size and SHA-256 |

**Scope:** v2.1 is an array-scale reference, one value per site at about 814,000 array CpGs; it holds no molecule-level (read-level) markers.

Values are stored as round(value x 10000) in unsigned 16-bit integers: value = stored / 10000 (exact to 4 decimals); **65535 = not measured**.
The 79 cells are split into three files in alphabetical order so every file stays under GitHub's 100 MB limit; join the parts side by side.

Checked 2026-10-16: every file matches its checksum, and on three cells at every site the copy differs from the full atlas by at most 0.00005
(the rounding). Made by `../../doors/data/DEV_ATLAS_V21_01/export_compact_v21.py` (rounding only). The full atlas file (2.4 GB, with donor
spread, R-hat and ESS per site) and the 100 posterior draws per block (24 GB) are public in Zenodo record [10.5281/zenodo.23422688](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23422688)
(ten bundles of 70 blocks, each file checked by `output_manifest_v21.json`); the fitted atlas is record [10.5281/zenodo.23441999](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23441999).

```python
import pandas as pd
sites = pd.read_parquet("sites.parquet").cpg
mu = pd.concat([pd.read_parquet(f"mu_part{n}.parquet") for n in (1, 2, 3)], axis=1)
mu.index = sites; mu = mu.where(mu != 65535) / 10000
```
